utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Karadzic. You have 30 minutes to conclude your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. I regret that I have to say for the record and for the sake of the truth, Your Honours, that so far we've had witnesses who were privy only to tiny pieces of the Sarajevo war puzzle. Now we have people, particularly this witness here, who was familiar with the entire puzzle, and I've only been granted 15 per cent of the requested time. So, regrettably, I will not be able to even touch upon some of the topics, let alone get to the bottom of them. So I'm really frustrated with the allocation of 15 per cent. Witness, sir, you -- you have provided two examples of sniping. Since we don't have time to go over more of them, I would like to focus on those two incidents or two incidents of sniping. Yesterday, we left it off with document 65 ter 16863. I don't know whether we tendered it into evidence or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it not part of Prosecution's associate exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's been admitted as Exhibit P2113.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this document has been admitted. Those are two example. The first one is the murder of Corporal Hardouin, and the second is a close-range shooting or opening fire on the PTT building. Witness, do you agree - you've already mentioned something to that effect - that every time it should be established where fire came from given the fact that the lines were very close and the fact that there were Muslim snipers positioned between us and the place of the incident or the target of the shooting.

utterances.speaker: KDZ304 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. 1D2982 is the document that I would like to call up. Let's identify the first page first -- first, and -- and see what is there. And while we are waiting, sir, in paragraph 16 of your statement -- or, rather, on page 16, paragraph 1, you conclude this: "[In English] To identify the persons responsible." [Interpretation] And this relates to the responsibility for the killing of Corporal Hardouin. And now could you please pay attention to this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be zoomed in? We don't have a Serbian version. We don't need a Serbian version at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 1, paragraph 1, you can see that a report was made [In English] Peacekeeping troops [Interpretation] In the United Nations unit trying to deal with the issue of Serb sniping at civilians: "[In English] ... have concluded that until mid-June, some gunfire also came from some gunmen soldiers deliberately shooting at their own civilians." [Interpretation] Can we now move on to page 4. Let's not waste too much time on this document. We will tender it, and then can we look at page 4, please. Is this page 4? I'm afraid -- can we -- previous page. Something with the page is wrong. [In English] Members of -- [Interpretation] Second paragraph: "[In English] Members of the United Nations Anti-sniping Unit who said they are equipped with infra-red and thermal viewing devices to watch suspected snipers' nests said they would begin their investigation after studying the trajectory of bullets striking near central Sarajevo. They concluded that some of the shooting was coming from the former parliament building. 'It was the only place where some of the snipers could be,' said a soldier on the investigating team." [Interpretation] Therefore, in your statement you say that you personally didn't see that. However, it is obvious that such things did happen; right? And that there were talks about that among the United Nations circles. And that's in your statement on page 13, paragraph 3, where you say that you didn't (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, the source of this information in a "New York Times" was a member of UN staff. Do you agree that even if you didn't observe things that they didn't happen?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, it is true that I didn't see or observe this. As for the investigations that were carried out, they were carried out in a very objective manner, and so various point of views were checked against each other. The journalist of the "New York Times" or the journalist of the "New York Times" has an opinion that he possibly only shares with himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: A redaction is required at page 3, lines 24, 25.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A bit lower down on the same page, Witness: "[In English] But the building is in the line between buildings from which Bosnian Serb snipers open fire, and areas of Sarajevo where many people have been shot." [Interpretation] I don't want to spend any more time on this document, but could you pay attention to these three paragraphs ending with the "Parliament building." Do you agree with me that all those investigations, not only of Muslim sniping but also of Serb sniping, did not follow a proper procedure, or in other terms, in the terms of proper criminal procedure, they were not carried out in the same way they would have been carried out in conditions of peace or in peacetime?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, you are right to underscore that the rules of criminal investigations were not applied, and they could not be applied given the attitude displayed by either one and the other party. And the journalist is right in saying that the various shooting positions of the ones and the others were very close. But I would like to remind you, and I'm sure you're very aware of this, that the survival condition of a sniper should be such that they have to be hidden in a second room in a building, and therefore their viewing angle, as well as their shooting angle, is very narrow. So how could you possibly conceive that snipers, and let's admit that they were Serb - this is just an example I'm giving you - could be positioned to shoot in the direction of the Bosnian Muslim people? How could you imagine or conceive that they could shoot behind them. This is impossible. And the same goes for Bosnian Muslim snipers. You could not shoot at the various directions when you are a sniper. This is how it works as a sniper. I hope that you understand this technical explanation. I'm sorry, but I feel that it was necessary to explain this given the statements that you have made.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: We object to the admission of this document. The witness hasn't confirmed any aspects, and, in fact, has stated that in his view it's the opinion of the journalist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Indeed. We do not admit this article.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The journalist does provide his source.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, Witness, do you agree that the political damage inflicted by sniping incidents, especially those that occurred around the Holiday Inn, that it was the Serbs who suffered political damage, whereas the Muslim side reaped benefits from those incidents in the international -- in the eyes of the international general public?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would concur with you that the Bosnian Muslim side was trying to use the attacks of which they were victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you also agree in general terms that those incidents inflicted huge political damage upon the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, with all due respect, I believe that you are wrong in your political assessment. The various measures that were taken in order to make the people of Sarajevo literally choke since the month of January, and I will give some examples: The increase of shots against the civilian population and therefore the increase of losses, the fact that blue routes could no longer be used for humanitarian aid. And I can also give you another example: The permanent ban of any use of public transport such as the tram in Sarajevo, which should not be construed as a military objective, as well as pumping from the Bosna River, and the supply and electricity, everything was designed in such a way that, in fact, it totally underestimated or did not estimate properly the psychological impact on the population. And the serious mistake in the end could be attributed to those who made the mistake in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, Witness, the Defence rejects all of those generalised allegations. We are trying to go straight into the heart of the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do not make your statement. Ask questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would kindly ask the witness to give us very specific examples instead of very generalised statements. But let's look at 65 ter 992 [as interpreted]. We are still talking about sniping one's own people. Let's look at the document, please. Let's look at page 1, 65 ter 9922. With all due respect, Your Excellency, generalised statements require more time. The Defence really cannot accept such generalised statements. Let's talk about very concrete examples. Let's identify this report from a meeting of the Army of Republika Srpska. Let's see if that is that. Can we now look at page 5 of the document. Page 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this not only of three pages? And I think it's prudent not to broadcast this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at bullet point B: "[In English] Discussion General Smith, General Clark." No, it's not on this page, I'm sure. I will read while the document is being produced: "[In English] General Delic reported to be frustrated at the state of BH sniping and firing incidents in Sarajevo area attributed to BH. Delic has given some -- given come command -- to the commandant at UNPROFOR his approval to return fire at any Bosnian ill discipline." [Interpretation] Does this passage show, Witness, that that matter was presented to General Delic by UNPROFOR, that that matter was presented to General Delic in the most official manner? He felt frustrated. He approved fire to be returned, just like General Mladic approved that UNPROFOR can open fire on Serbian positions every time needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Have we identified the passage?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The page number is ERN 1064581. In e-court the document is shorter. Early on there were six pages in e-court, and all of a sudden the document is shorter. 1064581.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're telling now it's different 65 ter number -- oh, ERN number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] ERN number. The page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can probably clarify here. There was an error with the upload of that document and the last three pages were removed a number of days ago because it concerned a separate meeting to the one that was discussed in the statement. Therefore, it wasn't appropriately tendered through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where are they now? Can you locate it now?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: We can locate that. Give us a few minutes. Maybe we can return to that topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Shall we move on to another topic in the meantime, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Thank you. And when we receive the document, we will just briefly show it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: One of the topics that I need to discuss with you, Witness, is the issue of investigations which were carried out by the United Nations. On page 15, paragraph 2, the penultimate paragraph from the bottom, you are talking about the hindrances posed to your investigations by the Bosnian side: "[In English] On the Serbian, access to the sites was bad, and on the Bosnian side where there was no rush to assist them, and in some cases their access to the sites was also hampered. In fact, both sides put obstacles against us." [Interpretation] Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that both sites were putting up numerous obstacles for investigation teams during that period of time, and we are talking about April, June, and July 1995, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to the fact that investigations were being hindered, the Muslim authorities also made three other things possible. They restricted your movements around city. They restricted your access to the hospitals and -- and they hindered your investigations on shelling incidents. The free -- the freedom of movement, instigation on the shelling incidents and access to -- to the hospitals; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And as far as Markale is concerned, we cannot go in depth of that matter due to the lack of time, but there is a part which might be of some assistance. You arrived in Markale, Markale II, within ten minutes of the explosion; right? Ten minutes after the explosion, you were at Markale; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A correction. I explained that I felt that I had arrived a few minutes after the explosion, without being able to say exactly how far after -- how long after the explosion I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you arrived, there, and we know that it didn't take a long time to get there. That's the question. Did it take you a long time to get there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, a short span of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you arrived there, the dead bodies and the injured had already been evacuated; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as most of the victims are concerned, that is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a few questions for you regarding the events which took place towards the end of May 1995, after your arrival in Sarajevo. Yesterday, we mentioned and you agreed that the Muslim offensive was launched in mid-May and that the BiH Army had some successes and that the offensive was rather fierce; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will repeat what I said yesterday. During the first few days, the forces of the 1st Corps of Bosnia-Herzegovina had scored some successes in two areas where the attack was focused.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked in the Milosevic trial, this is English transcript page 5372, whether, not you personally but the United Nations, or perhaps even you personally, whether you launched an attack on the BH Army because of the attacks that were launched in mid-May, and you (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Hayden, were you able to locate the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Give us 30 more seconds. And while I'm on my feet, a redaction at line 3 on page 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You remember that on the 15th of May, 1995, a total exclusion zone was in place banning the use of heavy weaponry inside the city, and also within a 20-kilometre radius; correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This offensive --

utterances.speaker: KDZ304 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... BH Army, and its use of heavy weapons violated this provision about the total exclusion zone; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Serbs, in keeping with the protocol and in keeping with the promises made to them, retrieved their weapons only after the Muslim offensive had started, retrieved them from under the UNPROFOR supervision.

utterances.speaker: KDZ304 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're wrong. You are wrong, because the first withdrawal of weapons was made in the week right after the launch of the offensive by blocking off a number of small units that were supposed to monitor these locations. The first blocking off of these small isolated units occurred on the 20 -- or the 20th or 21st of May. Then on the Bosna -- Bosnian Muslim side then these -- this blocking off became hostage-taking, and this was on May 26th and May 27th. What did this prove? Well, it simply proves that the tactical situation in Sarajevo was wrongly assessed. The superiority of the SRK was such that this could contain the offensive of the Bosnian Muslims without having to resort to infringements on the exclusion zone, and that is the error made by the command of the SRK.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: The document is now uploaded, 09922A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I will give you three more minutes to conclude your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at that document now. But many, many questions remain outstanding that we haven't had time to touch upon, and they follow from the examination-in-chief and from the statements of this witness. What are we going to do? Are we going to call him again? I'm afraid the Defence will have to ask for him to be recalled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the next page, the paragraph containing the reference to General Delic. In English it's page 2, "[In English] General Delic reported to be frustrated," [Interpretation] is the beginning of this paragraph. So this was presented in to General Delic. It was put to him in the most formal, in the most official way, at the highest level. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read this document, and I also put my signature on it. You can see it on the first page. So I have no reason to doubt that this was not shown to General Delic. But you must have understood that I did not attend this meeting myself between General Smith and General Delic. I wasn't there physically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did it happen that the UNPROFOR opened fire in May and August against the positions of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In May, no. The first shots occurred as of June 10 or 11 when a heavy mortar battery was transported to Mount Igman. Let me remind you that it was -- the fire was opened not as -- not to punish the SRK, as you said yesterday, but in a very measured fashion and cautious fashion, in a moderate fashion. The first shots were always fired on my order, as close as possible to the positions that had been targeted, and there was always prior notice. There was always a few seconds or a few minutes of prior notice. So we would always notice the staff at Lukavica before firing. We would always give them advance notice. And these were shots fired from modern artillery that can target immediately without having to fire some adjustments shots, which was the case for the SRK artillery. And therefore, these shots never hit the target. Either they were smokescreens or other kind of shots, but they were always in the surrounding of the position targeted, and they were always after giving notice to the staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, your last question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I hope -- I beg you to reconsider and give us at least 20 minutes. There's a huge number of questions that are outstanding, and they do follow from -- from the statements of this witness. And while you take time to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic. The Chamber gave consideration to the matter. You could ask those questions yesterday. Your last question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I haven't been able to ask them all because of the lengthy answers of the witness, whom I appreciate and respect, but if this is the last question ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true, Witness, that the UNPROFOR, during these misunderstandings with the Bosnian Serb Army, took members of the VRS prisoner even during May 1995? Did the UNPROFOR and the VRS take each other's members prisoners?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know very well that after the traitorous aggression of the units of Commander Kovacevic, who was in charge of the Grbavica Battalion, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: KDZ304 [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted) they were accommodated in a very comfortable fashion and while respecting all rules on the Sarajevo airstrip before we hand them back over to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I just have one more question to clear this up?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Another witness here, Francis Roy Thomas, confirmed that on Vrbanja Bridge the Muslim army camouflaged themselves and wore French uniforms to be able to get close to the VRS, up to 3 metres.

utterances.speaker: KDZ304 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is ludicrous. This is false. This is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Apologies for the interruption. Can we have a reference for this statement attributed to Francis Roy Thomas?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the witness has answered the question already and it's not necessary. Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. Mr. Hayden, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour, and before --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document be admitted? Let me inform Mr. Hayden that it's in the transcript. I have no time, but it's in the transcript that Francis Roy Thomas came --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's not necessary --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- came 3 metres close to them when he realised that they were, in fact, Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will admit 65 ter 9922A as the Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D959.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That can be a public document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Morrison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, when you gave the answer in respect to the last question from Dr. Karadzic, you said it's -- it's false. This is wrong. Did you mean to say that the idea that that could have happened was wrong, or were you referring to the testimony of Mr. Thomas himself, in other words, that Mr. Thomas didn't say it, or that if Mr. Thomas did say it then it was false and wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, from what I understood, I understood that the ABiH soldiers had -- were wearing French uniforms in order to come closer to our positions or to the Serbian positions in Vrbanja, and I confirm that this is wrong. This is false.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Before I begin redirect examination, there's a redaction required at line -- page -- let me -- sorry, I'm just scrolling up, Mr. President. Page 14, lines 19 to 22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness. Yesterday, Mr. Karadzic discussed with you what he described as a protocol. This, for the record, is Exhibit D717. And at transcript page 10510, he said that according to this protocol, the Bosnian Serb Army had the right to implement measures of self-defence in certain circumstances, and that's what they were doing when they undertook actions in May 1995, and again he repeated that this morning at transcript page 11, line 20. He said that the actions that led to NATO intervention were, in fact, actions taken in accordance with this alleged protocol. Now, you said yesterday at transcript page 10501 that you were not familiar with this protocol, and I'd like to explore the reasons why you're not familiar with this protocol. Now, at -- in your statement, you make reference to the mandate of UNPROFOR in Sarajevo, and you say that one of the four missions of the battalions in Sarajevo was supervision of agreements, and you list as an example the agreement of February 1994. Mr. Witness, was it the case that you were expected to supervise all operative agreements between the United Nations and the warring parties in Sarajevo, or if I can put it another way, all agreements that had legal standing between the United Nations and the warring parties? Was that the case?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayden. I was -- I must confess I was a bit surprised by this question yesterday. Our mission, of course, was to monitor this, and of course I wasn't -- I -- I wasn't -- these texts were known to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: If I can ask for 65 ter 23071, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. While that's being brought up, I wonder if the Prosecution can indicate to us is it their case that the United Nations was not obligated to honour that agreement that we have in front of us, signed by the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I'm happy to answer that question, Mr. President, and it may become clearer once I'm finished with my redirect examination what the position of the Prosecution is on this very point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: This, Mr. Witness, is a code cable from Mr. Akashi to Mr. Annan in New York. It's sent on 12th of September, 1994, which precedes your time, but it does discuss the protocol that was discussed yesterday. If we look in the first paragraph, it states that -- in the second sentence: "We have also conducted a legal review of the protocol we forwarded in the code cable of 16 August 1994." It makes the point in the second paragraph that while the points of agreement that had the signatures of the United Nations appended to it is validated, that the protocol, in contrast, was a Bosnian Serb proposal was never accepted by it us, and it goes on to say it was sent in error. And if I can draw your attention to the final paragraph which summarises the advice of the United Nations in summary the protocol has no legal standing. Mr. Witness, if a protocol had no legal standing in the view of UNPROFOR headquarters, would you have expected to know about such an agreement or be expected to enforce it?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know this text, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Aside from the text, Mr. Witness, and of course you would never have seen this code cable, but in the abstract, if an agreement had no legal standing, would UNPROFOR headquarters have instructed you to enforce or supervise such an agreement?

utterances.speaker: KDZ304 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our mission was simple. We were there to monitor the weapons and make sure that they could not be used by the SRK units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: That concludes the redirect examination. If the Bench has any further questions about our position on this matter in light of Mr. Robinson's intervention, then we're happy to assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that answers my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I may now read a summary of the written evidence in a language the witness understands. I'll begin. [Interpretation] During the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the witness was part of the UNPROFOR in the Sarajevo sector from 1993 until 1994. During his mission in Sarajevo, the witness was able to note that the local population was very often harassed by shellings with heavy weapons which -- which wanted to harass the local population, intimidate it, and hinder the normal daily life of this population. According to the witness, the shellings and the snipings were tactical means for the Bosnian Serbs. They wanted put a term to the offensive of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and they were also strategic in order to force the representatives of the Bosnian Muslims to accept the territorial division of Sarajevo and of Bosnia. According to the information that were given to him, the witness was able to establish a correlation between the increase of the offensive launched by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the whole of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the attacks launched against the civilian population in Sarajevo. Indeed, most shellings and most snipings did take place after offensives had been launched by the Muslims. Therefore, these were retaliations, and he thought that the orders for the retaliations were given by higher echelon to the commanding officers. After the shelling and the snipings, protests were sent either to the 1st Corps of the -- of the ABiH or to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Usually they ignored the process and didn't take them seriously, and when they responded, when they replied to them, they rejected all responsibility. After the bombing of Markale in January -- in February 1994, negotiations started to take place in Sarajevo in order to implement a cease-fire. Most meetings did take place whilst the witness attended these meetings. During these meetings, he met several times Stanislav Galic, the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and between the month August and September 1994, he met his successor Dragomir Milosevic. He met him two or three times. In -- when we think about the chain of command of the Bosnian Serbs, as far as the witness understood it, the corps commander -- commanders had very -- could take few initiatives. According to him, they were always obeying the orders of their commanding officer, Ratko Mladic. General Rose and Radovan Karadzic, did also take part in the negotiations. [In English] That concludes the summary of the written evidence, Your Honours. Now, Mr. Witness, I wonder to begin if you could describe for us the types of information available to you during your time in Sarajevo as regards the situation there.

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: Yes. In order to answer this question, I would like to go to closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We are now in open session, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Witness, you've noted in your written evidence at paragraph 24 that there were three main periods to your mandate. Are you able to describe or outline those periods for us?

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: Yes, I can do that. I'm sorry, it may take some time, but I think I should give some specifications about this period between October 1993 and September 1994, and this is what I would like to say about this period: Between October 1993 until the 5th February 1994, this was a very difficult period. And it was particularly difficult for the Sarajevo population, because there were numerous snipers attacks. There were quite a lot of heavy weapons shellings, and it was very difficult for the humanitarian supply. It was the second winter of the siege, and the population was already pretty exhausted. So the operations had resumed, and I think that they had resumed because there was failure, the failure of the agreement Owen-Stoltenberg in September. So this was for the first period. As far as the second period is concerned, between the 5th February and the end of the month of July, I will tell you that this was a period of relative stability. There was the total exclusion area for heavy weaponry, a cease-fire after the 5th of February, and the opening of the blue routes, which enabled to stabilise the humanitarian situation, and the military situation. There was no more shelling during that period. The town was not shelled any more, and there were some sniping activities which were very few and which started again towards the end of the period but not in a heavy way. From the end of July 1994 until the end of September, I will say that this was a very uncertain period. There was diplomatic activity underway, because you had the peace plan which had been put forward by the Contact Group and had been turned down by the Serbs, and at that time there was a deterioration of the situation with more sniping activities, with the closing up of the open routes, and a general deterioration of the situation. This is in a nutshell the three periods that we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to go back to a couple of aspects of your answers, you seem to have made a linkage between -- on the one hand, between the situation in Sarajevo, on the one hand, with the failure of the Owen-Stoltenberg agreement, and on the other hand, the failure of the Contact Group plan. In other words, diplomatic events, political events. Did you see the situation in Sarajevo as being affected by any other external factors?

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned the diplomatic or political events, but, of course, as far as the situation in Sarajevo was concerned, it was also affected by the military operations. So we could say that there were military operation on the front lines that circled Sarajevo. There were also military operations for the whole of Bosnia. And whenever an offensive was launched by the Muslim forces in order to break the siege of Sarajevo, there were Serb reactions in order to defend themselves. So we had military operations on the front lines, on the confrontation lines, but also on the Sarajevo population. But in times when the Sarajevo sector was calm, we saw sniping activities, or we saw that shots were being fired at the population, and we received the different reports on the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And this is when we realised that there was a link, a correlation between the Sarajevo actions and an offensive which could be launched elsewhere in Bosnia-Herzegovina, on the Brcko corridor, for instance, on Doboj, for instance, or around Maglaj, i.e., outside the Sarajevo area. And this is why we thought that there were links between the military operations in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the reactions from the Bosnian Serbs in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To your mind, what kind of command level does this correlation that you've described implicate?

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: This means that when there was an attack outside Sarajevo, there was a reaction, and this could only be organised by the high military command, the command -- the high command in Sarajevo could not take the initiative to react to an action that was no concern to them. And I think it was General Karadzic, in fact, who was telling them, act on Sarajevo in order to exert pressure on the Bosnian Muslim authorities so that they stop their actions elsewhere in Bosnia-Herzegovina. For me, it was very -- it was crystal clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, the clock on my computer says 10.27. Would it be appropriate to stop now for the break before moving on to another area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To continue, Mr. Witness, you noted at paragraphs 30 and 31 of your written evidence that on a number of occasions you were present during meetings and discussions with -- in which the Bosnian Serb political and military leaders took part in with other interlocutors, and I wonder if you could put those meetings in context for us. utterances.speaker: KDZ450

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to the subject of sniping now and ask whether on the basis of the information in your possession and your personal observations you developed an opinion on the skill level of the snipers operating in Bosnian-Serb held territory.

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: Snipers were very well trained from a military point of view. They had undergone some training. They had precision weapons. They had done a very rigorous training in order to use these weapons appropriately. So one could say that they were very professional in their job as snipers. In other words, they did not become snipers in an improvised manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What do you base this on?

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: I base this on the fact that they were able to reach very small sized targets and sometimes not very visible at very large distances, which can only be achieved by highly experienced and trained marksmen. And I have an example of a young Blue Helmet from a French battalion. I believe that it happened on the 18th of August, 1994, and he was shot in the head while he was in the frame of a window of about 20 centimetres, 27 centimetres. It was a very small window. He was observing from there. And the marksman, or the sniper, that is, was probably more than 200 or 300 metres apart from the Blue Helmet that was shot, so this required very, very high skills.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could go into private session for the next area, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, to move to another topic, that would be the 20 kilometre total exclusion zone and the weapons collection points that were instituted around Sarajevo in 1994, perhaps I could ask you the following: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: To answer this question, I would prefer to go back to private session because I took part in those discussions, but in my capacity.
