utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, as I was reading your statement, I noted that you're capable of providing very brief answers in view of the brevity of time given to me, I'm going to try and put very simple questions to you in order to enable you to answer by just saying yes or no. I would also like you to understand that the Defence needs to make a distinction between those parts of your statements which are based on your sentiments and assumptions, on the one hand, and those that are based on your first-hand knowledge gained from documents. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: Accused, since you're called that way, I do answer concisely, but I never answer a question by yes or no because these are complicated circumstances. So I would like to keep my freedom of speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Defence will certainly agree to that and will not object. In your statements, you, yourself, indicate what your personal feelings are, which is very fair. Let's look at your statement provided on the 5th of July, 2000.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The exhibit number is 1D3074 [as interpreted], page 10, paragraph 2. I can read: "[In English] For example, if Karadzic could order attacks on Sarajevo simply to prove something, he could request his soldiers to put on a show of strength at Sarajevo and so draw the press attention to the region ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Nobody sees the document on e-court in front of them, and I have a copy in French of that statement for the witness. Maybe that might, at least, help him provide an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But what is 1D3074?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3004. That's the paragraph that I'm reading from. The statement itself is voluminous, but I just wanted that paragraph. 004 is the entire statement -- actually, 3004, and on page 10, paragraph 2, is what I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's upload it. Ms. Edgerton -- you have the French version of this?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I have the original version in his own language for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the Defence does not mind, why don't you hand it over to the witness. Do you have original version in e-court as well?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It should not be broadcast. In English it's what we see on the screen; page 10, paragraph 2, actually. It's the right document, but we need page 10, paragraph 2, and in French it might be 11 or 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the middle of paragraph 2: "[In English] For example, Karadzic could order attacks on Sarajevo simply to prove something. He could request his soldiers to put on a show of strength at Sarajevo and so draw the press's attention to the region."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "[In English] But that is purely my only personal feeling." [Interpretation] Do you want by what you stated here, "[In English] But that is only my personal feeling," [Interpretation] or is there any corroboration of that? There are more things, namely that it was never said to you by the corps commander, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: Earlier on, I said that we drew some conclusions. And when I say "we," it's a collective "we." The siege of Sarajevo had one main goal, to exert pressure on the Bosnian Muslims' authorities. This is what I would like to summarise in a few words. And it was a conclusion that we drew from several observations, as I've already explained to you earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just again for the record in French it's on the page numbered R0658113.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come back to the issue of the siege of Sarajevo, but this says that it was your own personal feeling, and that's what I'm interested in. In cases like this, can we distinguish between your personal feelings and guesswork from what is -- can be reliably proven by documents?

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: I shall repeat what I've already said. We made an assessment of the siege of Sarajevo from the -- from what we could see inside the Sarajevo confrontation line, and we also observed was happening on the general theatre in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We also drew conclusions about the links between the military situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the military, political, and diplomatic situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tender this paragraph, the page?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's included in full in the amalgamated document at paragraph 33.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure the consolidated statement contains these key words about personal feeling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it does. Take a look. It says: "For example, Karadzic could order attacks on Sarajevo simply to prove something."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That's possible. There are several statements, and these statements are organised in different ways. Sometimes the answers are very brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I now draw your attention to the next page, page 11, paragraph 2. [No interpretation]: "[In English] I got the impression that every time we wanted to ask the corps commander for something, he had to ask Mladic. The corps commander couldn't apparently use his initiative at all. If attacked, he could counter-attack, but he could not use his initiative and start a confrontation. This is just my own feeling." [Interpretation] Is this right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: This is what is written, but what I meant by these words is that the corps could only take an initiative in order to return fire on his sector, but when they had to launch an action with the soldiers on Sarajevo and when there was a link with an operation outside Sarajevo, he was receiving orders from the higher command, i.e., from Mladic. In other words, he could not have taken the initiative to act within the confrontation line inside Sarajevo in order to return fire after an action which had been launched outside that same perimeter. That's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I now ask for 1D3006. It's another one of your statements of 21 November 2007. It should not be broadcast. Page 9, paragraph 2. At page 9, please, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Page 9 doesn't have a paragraph 2. It has a paragraph 34, 35, and 36.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's see page 9 and then we'll see. "[In English] First of all" -- [Interpretation] This paragraph, I meant, that starts with "First of all." The second answer: "[In English] First of all, I have no evidence or material trace of the orders regarding the shelling of all the sniping against civilians. I think, and this is a thought, that the orders regarding shelling and sniping against civilians came from a high level within the army." [Interpretation] Is this right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: I repeat once more that I drew this conclusion after my General Staff and myself came to this these conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 1D3007 is the next document we need, your statement from 2009; page 2, answer B: "[In English] What in your view, was the role of Radovan Karadzic? And why?" [Interpretation] Answer: "[In English] This led us to believe that the orders for measures of retaliation against the population of Sarajevo came from a -- a level higher than the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, VRS. I cannot tell you anything specific about the role of Radovan Karadzic in the chain of command that ordered the measures of retaliation." [Interpretation] Is this right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: Yes. This reply summarises the way I saw the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to ask you if you agree that the supreme commander and the political chief of the United Nations army was the Secretary-General himself and his main representative on the ground was Mr. Akashi?

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: I understood that the Security Council had -- was responsible for this. The Secretary-General has to implement the decisions taken by the Security Council of the United Nations, and the special representative was the representative of the Secretary-General, so he was a man who was close to the theatre of operations and close to UNPROFOR, and he did convey to UNPROFOR the decisions and resolutions of the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that it was Ambassador Akashi who talked to Radovan Karadzic, and the commander of the Sarajevo zone talked to the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: I would like to say something about the notion of negotiation. As far as I'm concerned, you negotiate with an enemy, but we were nobody's enemy. We were there to discuss, to talk, and this is quite different. So we talked with the different parties. And it is true to say that Mr. Akashi spoke with the accused, and as I -- and as you've just told us, the commander for -- the BH commander talked with the Commander-in-Chief of the forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall I go back -- go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that apart from talks, and I accept these were not negotiations, but talks, talks leading to agreements, do we agree with that, that our discussions led to a variety of agreements?

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that on the operative and tactical levels I met with the officers of the United Nations at their own request when it was necessary to deal with a controversial situation?

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: I do not know whether this was at their request, but I can certainly concur with you. You met civilian and military authorities of UNPROFOR, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you accept that a civilian head of state and civilian commander of the army, just like Mr. Akashi himself, does not deal with operative or tactical issues, only strategic issues?

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: I do not understand the difference that you are making between strategical, operational and tactical.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said today that I took part in some negotiations on major issues, and one of those issues was the total exclusion zone. I want to move to that subject, and I want to ask you whether Mr. Akashi ever dealt with minor operative or technical -- tactical issues concerning the troops of the United Nations, or he left it to professional officers.

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: He used to work in close co-operation with the military people in charge, because for every decision about military or diplomatic actions, there was a convergence of endeavours made by the diplomatic, political, and military authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that one of those major agreements that required the presence of Mr. Akashi and myself was the agreement on the total exclusion zone?

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: Are you talking about the agreement of the 18th of February? We talked about it earlier on, and the document was submitted to me earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I remember the signature of this agreement, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since I was not precise enough in my previous question, was the presence of Mr. Akashi and myself necessary to deal with the minor issues that were part of that agreement, or did everyone deal with that at their own level?

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: The presence of high civilian authorities as yourself and of the special representative who represented the international community at the time gave quite a certain importance to this agreement, and it gave the agreement it's force, its strength. But afterwards, there were discussions among the Romanija Corps and within the Sector Sarajevo in order to specify some minor details, or some details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I now call D1 -- sorry, D717, and we've seen it today. It was called up by Mrs. Edgerton. Page 3 of this document. This is the agreement that Ambassador Akashi and myself signed on the 18th of February. Do you agree that this form of agreement, the language, the structure and the terminology of this text were created by the UN services?

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: I do not really understand the question that you've just asked. Could you rephrase your question so I could understand what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'll try. Do you agree that this document was developed by the service of Ambassador Akashi? They created the document, and we signed it.

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: It was drafted after discussions took place. This was not a document that was put forward by UNPROFOR. It didn't happen so often. There was a proposal, then there were talks about it, and I guess that the authorities of the Bosnian Serbs said, We want to change this, modify that and the other, and then we had this agreement. This is quite classical in terms of agreement between two people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But the drafting itself, who drafted this agreement? Let me remind you. Behind the number 18, for instance, in our language, in the date, 18 February, there would be a dot after 18 if it was made by -- by the Serb side. Do you agree that the UN side drafted the document?

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether you're asking me a question or you're stated a fact, but what I can tell you, in order to give you more information, is that the initiative of this agreement came from UNPROFOR. That's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Next page, please. I was talking about the technical aspect of the -- of the drafting, and I am saying that it's the United Nations who drafted the document, chose the wording, typed it, et cetera. Now, look at this protocol. Just a moment. Do you see the top of the document, was it sent from BH command? If we can see the very top of the document. The fax identification is at the very top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just we need to show the top part. Scroll up. If you could zoom up -- zoom in a bit further so that the witness can see the upper part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see it's from BH command? The facsimile identification.

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: Yes, I see that it's written "From BH Command, Sarajevo," but I see the date of August, 1994, 14 hours 33.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask you to look at numbers 1994. There is no dot after that number. And the 15th of February, "Subsequent meeting": "[In English] This meeting produced a three-point agreement signed by Mr Akashi and Dr. Karadzic. See Annex A. At a subsequent meeting on 19th of February, it was further agreed that ..." [Interpretation] And then follows what was agreed as part of the protocol. Do you see that, and do you agree that after all these sequential numbers and dates there is no dot? And the last sentence here in the first paragraph here, does it say this: "[In English] A subsequent meeting on 19th of February, it was further greed that ..."?

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: Yes, I read what is written, and what I know about this document is that it was not signed -- that no one signed it. And it is said earlier on or later on. I guess it was a proposal put forward by the Bosnian Serbs during the meeting of the 18th of February. But this proposal was neither signed nor agreed upon by Mr. Akashi. But of course this document could have well been taken back to the BH commander who then relayed it during the month of August in order to give some explanations. This is what I can see from this document, from reading this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the second page of the same document. Let's look at the state of consciousness of Ambassador Akashi, or the state of mind of Ambassador Akashi. Witness, I claim that this was created by the United Nations, that this was in force. The protocol did not have to be signed because the basic document was signed, and this was just its annex. Let's look at the entire second page of the document. With can see here Lukavica 19 February, no dot after the 19th, and the wording, the language is of the kind used by the United Nations. Right. This is how texts were drafted or have been -- are still drafted in the United Nations; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: I'm afraid I cannot give any information as to the way this document was drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we look at the second page of the entire document, which means that we have to go three pages back, four pages back. Look at paragraph 3 here: "[In English] The protocol for the Sarajevo WCP Agreement of 14th of February 1994 (attached) recognises the BSA's legitimate right of self-defence. If the BSA comes under more pressure from the BiH, their demand to have access to their weapons could become a more pressing reality, under the protocol referred to above."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm waiting for the interpretation to be finished. I don't want to overlap with the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this beyond any reasonable doubt the state of mind that prevailed in the United Nations? Mr. Akashi was named here, Mr. Stoltenberg was informed, and there must have been somebody who prepared this letter for Mr. Akashi; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, questions about the state of mind of the United Nations really do call for speculation on the part of the witness, I would think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I rephrase the question? Mr. Witness, this -- this document was drafted by Mr. Akashi, as you saw. Do you remember that? Shall I show you the first page of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I have no detail as to whether it was drafted by Mr. Akashi, but also we're talking about a date of the 14th agreement -- the 14th of February for an agreement. I don't think there was an agreement on the 14th of February. The first agreement was signed on the 18th of February, so you see that in this paragraph it is -- there is a date of the 14th of February and I don't believe that there was a agreement by then. So perhaps it is a document that was prepared, a working document, and maybe it never came into force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question is this: As we see page 3 -- can you show the witness, please. Points of agreement, three points of agreement was signed by Mr. Akashi in February. And shall we go back to the first page of this document. And Mr. Akashi sent this cable to Mr. Annan in August, from Mr. Akashi, UNPROFOR Zagreb. Can you scroll up? Yes. Next page. In this document, paragraph 3, Mr. Akashi refers to the protocol, and he further elaborates on this. Had he signed the three points agreement, he should have known that this protocol was not signed. So I take it Mr. Karadzic was asking why. Was it out of mistake on the part of Akashi, or can you explain? Help us in this regard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm very sorry, Your Honour, but I cannot give you any further details to clear this confusion in terms of date or in terms of the way those documents were drafted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember that the talks started on the 14th of February and finished on the 18th of February by signing?

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: Yes. Negotiations -- or, rather, talks lasted for several days. I would concur with you that the talks lasted for several days between the various participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at the first page again, because there's something in keeping with -- there with your words. Page 1, paragraph 2 speaks about the pressure of the Muslim army from the Visoko-Olovo-Kladanj axis. Do you remember that the Muslim artillery was in a position to open artillery fire in the total exclusion zone from the very border of that zone because those weapons had never been removed and in that respect they had an advantage over us?

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: I do not have any specific recollection regarding this point that you have just raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement and earlier today, I believe you mentioned pressures come -- coming from the outside of the exclusion zone from the Muslim side on the Serb side, but let's move on. Do you remember that was on the 19th of February, Lukavica, and that the protocol was the result of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't know. I think there might be something missing here, because we talked about pressures coming from outside the exclusion zone and that that was on the 19th of February at Lukavica. So I think we might be missing a line somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The explanation follows. Mr. Akashi wrote in on the 6th of February, and he says that at that time the Muslim army put pressure on the Serb army from outside of the exclusion zone, which can lead to -- to a situation where the Serbs will want to take their weapons back. Since no weapons were removed from outside the exclusion zone, they can still open fire, and Ambassador Akashi said that those actions provoked a realistic provocation wish for tactical gains. And if they continued, in paragraph 2: "[In English] Should the BH move heavy weapons into the zone, this would put them in clear violation of the EZ. In recent days, the BH have also fired weapons already within the zone. BH activity has already prompted the BSA to seek to withdraw their heavy weapons from the WCPs." [Interpretation] The fact of the matter is that they did not have to bring their weapons into the total exclusion zone in order to open fire on us who were within the total exclusion zone. We can show the map later. Is that correct, Witness? They were in a position to fire at us from within the exclusion zone as well as from outside of the exclusion zone? We couldn't return that fire, because our weapons had been seized from us.

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: On that date the ultimatum had not been agreed upon, which means that weapons were not under control, which means that what you said is not correct. The end of the ultimatum was on the 20th of February, so we were in a period of time where there were talks, and the Bosnian Serbs, as well as the Bosnian Muslims, had not sent their weapons to weapons collection points, which means that your questions should not have been asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm afraid I was not clear again. Mr. Akashi wrote on the 16th of August and mentioned recent fighting, and he says on the 6th and -- of -- and those were zones in contact with the exclusion zone where we no longer had our heavy weaponry at our disposal, whereas they were in a position to have their heavy weaponry at their disposal only a metre away from the border of the total exclusion zone. Can we now go back to the fourth page of the same document just to establish something. Can we look at the last sentence in the first paragraph. "[In English] On 19th of February, it was further agreed that ..." [Interpretation] Can we go briefly into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: (redacted) [Confidentiality partially lifted by order of the Chamber] now go to the following page, please. Bullet point 7, subparagraph B, where it says "Warring factions movements." And can we look at the comment: "[In English] This is further evidence of BSA withdrawals of equipment out of the 20 kilometres zone. These weapons will probably remain closed to the 20 kilometres limits so they can be deployed to react to any B and H aggression." [Interpretation] Do you agree, do you agree that this document also implies that the Serb side would be allowed to deploy their weaponry only if they came under attack from the BiH Army?

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: Of course. Weaponry outside the TEZ, namely the total exclusion zone, could allow the Serb to deploy those weapons if they came under attack from the BH Army outside the TEZ. And this explains why earlier on you said that regarding Visoko, Olovo, the Serbs as a retaliation in August 1994 against the BiH, the Serbs used weapons that were outside the TEZ. So there you go. That's what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The way we interpret this comment is different, because it says here that it may be deployed to react. If we look at the protocol and the telegram sent on the 20th, it is clear that the Serb side could not be forbidden to defend itself. Do you agree with me, Witness, that the heavy weaponry was the only element of strategic balance in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we can go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we are still in private session, and the interpreters didn't seem to catch all of your question. Could you repeat the last part of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we are in private session. This document does not say that it will happen but that it may be deployed, that the weaponry may be deployed in reaction to an aggression not outside of the exclusion zone but in the exclusion zone itself. This is a sequence of events. On the 14th, negotiations started. On the 18th, the agreement was concluded. The protocol was signed on the 20th, and then the telegram was sent to imply that the Serb had the right to self-defence; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Should I clarify with the witness further, or shall I leave it to the interpreters so that they can correct the interpretation later on. Thank you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, was it also the case in the exclusion zone around Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: This is not as clear in my mind, but the spirit of the exclusion zone in Gorazde was copied from what was in place in Sarajevo. However, contrary to what was happening in Sarajevo in the exclusion zone of Gorazde, there was no collection point for heavy weaponry. The monitoring was done by the UNMOs, and then later on by UNPROFOR units who entered the Gorazde area. But there was no weapon collection zone for heavy weapons in that area. That's the difference between the two.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would move to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D962, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we find another document, you'll see that Mr. Akashi and General Rose said that around Gorazde we had the right, unless protect by UNPROFOR, to take hold of our weapons. When I found -- find this document, we'll show you that. Likewise, the exclusion zone of 20 kilometres from Sarajevo was copied and applied in Gorazde. Let me ask you this, Mr. Witness: Did the BiH Army in the city of Sarajevo have any heavy weapons even though the exclusion zone applied to them as well?

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: Yes. There was one weapons collection point for heavy weapons held by Bosnian Muslims inside Sarajevo, but this was controlled by the UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: (redacted). You talked about shelling. Shelling means a great amount of shells, and if I remember well, there was only one attack, one shell that landed on the airport. The airport was not persistently shelled. Of course it was with weapons that had been concealed. Of course you must understand that this was a conflict where everyone was trying to trick the different parties, and one of the parties was the UNPROFOR. So we were trying to keep our eyes open, of course, but there were so many weapons, you know, in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Let me remind you in Bosnia-Herzegovina their conception -- their -- for them to defend themselves, they wanted to have all sorts of warehouses and ammunition warehouses and weapons in order to defend themselves. And you know that Bosnia-Herzegovina is very mountainous. It was very easy to conceal heavy weapons in that region.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But it says here that occasionally they shelled the airport. Did it ever happen that the Bosnian side was punished for this? Did NATO at the -- UNPROFOR's initiative punish the Bosnian Muslim side as it punished the Serbian side wherever it could?

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: The situation was as follows: When the airport was shot at or shelled, the only person in danger here were soldiers, UNPROFOR, but the civilian population was not targeted there, and that's a big difference.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just interested in knowing when does the Trial Chamber plan to take a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Whenever it is convenient. We'll have ten minutes 'break. Shall we take it -- think of --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Any time. Any time. It's all the same to the Defence. We can do it now, before we start another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wanted to tell you that we are still in private session. Shall we go back to open session?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have a break. --- Break taken at 1.41 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, with your guidance and of that of Mr. Doraiswamy, I sorted myself out on the 65 ter number you queried me about earlier on, 10920 is indeed a duplicate of P00861. And while I'm on my feet, 09658 is not a duplicate of P00862 and I would seek to tender that as an associated exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're referring to 09658?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Correct. I had wrongly indicated it was a duplicate of [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But is it referred to in his amalgamated statement? Could you take a look at it again?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Indeed, and I'm very sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just one question that I have already put but the interpreters did not get to interpret it. Do you agree that the BH Army had as many as three times more infantry than the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: Generally speaking, I cannot say that it was three times more, but the forces of the BH Army were -- were numerous in terms of infantry than that of the VRS. However, the VRS compensated this by a greater use of heavy weaponry, and they had more heavy weaponry than the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that the position of heavy weaponry was the only element of strategic balances between these two corps, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps on the one hand and the 1st Corps of the BH Army on the other?

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: The point was not to maintain a strategic balance. The point was to find a solution that would make -- that would help the population live in peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We can agree on that. However, my question was this: When it comes to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, did it become more vulnerable when its heavy weaponry as the only element of strategic control -- strategic balance was placed under control? And in that, the surplus of infantry of the BiH Army was not placed under any control.

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: My answer would be no. First, there was a cease-fire in place while there was a collection of heavy weapons in the WCPs. There was also a cease-fire in the sector of Sarajevo. Therefore, neither the BH Army nor the VRS advanced or made movement on the confrontation lines. The confrontation line stayed stable over that period. Therefore, this was not an advantage or disadvantage for any of the warring parties in Sector Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you saying that this would have been the case if the cease-fire was honoured?

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: No. This was the situation prevailing in Sarajevo. The cease-fire on shooting by heavy weapons did not do anything. It only -- it only made casualties among either civilians or military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour. I think the witness said the cease-fire on shooting in Sarajevo did absolutely not affect the situation in the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, can you confirm what Ms. Edgerton just now said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. The cease-fire and the collection of heavy weapons had no impact on the military situation in the city and outside the -- and around the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If the cease-fire had been complied with, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps would not have been put in an inferior position. But let me ask you this: If the numerous infantry had violated the cease-fire and if it had launched attacks on the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps that would not have been a position to defend itself by heavy weaponry, would that mean that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and the settlements under its protection would have been jeopardised? I'm talking only about the conduct of the Muslim infantry.

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: Well, I am not here to answer guesses and assumptions. What I realised is that during this period there was a part of the Muslim forces that left Sarajevo, and it might be that these forces had -- were used in order to fight outside the Sarajevo area. That's the only thing I can say, and it's what I said earlier on. This agreement had no impact whatsoever about -- on the military situation and on the military positions inside Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the situation change in a situation where the Muslim army attacked Serbs with their heavy weaponry within the total exclusion zone?

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: There was no such attack apart from in September. There was no heavy weapon attacks inside the Sector Sarajevo. But on the other hand, there was on the 18th of December of 1994, there was an escalation of violence, but in Sarajevo, or, around Sarajevo during this period there was no attack. There was only sniping activities, that's all. No offensive whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me remind you. You are speaking about the three main periods during your tour of duty. The first one was from the month of April -- or, rather, the last four months of 1993 up to February 1994. The next one -- this is your statement provided in 2007. If we have to put it on the screen, it is 1D3006, but let me read it instead: "[In English] There were three main periods during my mandate between the last four mandates of 1994. On 3 January and up to 5th of February, 1994, there was an increasing incident of shellings and sniping against the civilian population up to the firing of a mortar shell on the Markale Market on 5th of February, 1994."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, that was the first thing Ms. Edgerton dealt with when she started her examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Precisely. That has been confirmed. Let's go on to the second and the third periods which you marked as periods of more heavy fire. Let's go back to your claim that there was sniping incidents and shelling of the civilian population. Could you please pay attention to your statement with regard to the papal visit. Do you remember the Serbian side offered guarantees for the terrestrial corridor between Kiseljak and Sarajevo, Sarajevo as a result of the fact that the -- it was convinced that the papal aircraft would have been hit by the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. I remember that Monsignor Monterelli [phoen] told me that the Pope would not come because Bosnian Serbs could not guarantee his safety during his visit, and this I remember vividly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, very well. We'll have documents about that at some opportunity. Our fear was that the aircraft would be grounded, but we offered a helicopter to transport him from Split to Kiseljak. You may not remember that, but that was the case. But do you remember that the Pope visited Sarajevo in 1996, after the war?

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: I remember that the Pope went to Sarajevo, but I do not remember the details, because I was far away from that theatre of operation at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Muslim police detected a bomb which was intended for the Pope by the road that he was supposed to take? It was the Muslim police and the bomb was Muslim, and the bomb was intended for the Pope. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Before you answer. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 1994 or 1996? What year is he even talking about in posing this question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We don't see the relevance of the issue itself. Move on to your next topic, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just one question: Did the Muslims open fire on the helicopter, and did they -- that -- portray that as the Serbs shooting at the helicopter? And that was even before 1994, even before that period.

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... understand the question, because you haven't given me any time reference. When did they shoot at -- on a helicopter? Why? How?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In May 1994, Muslims opened fire on a UN helicopter; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: But where did they do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From Mount Igman.

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: It is possible, but I do not remember this. There was no victim. The helicopter didn't go down. Unfortunately, this was not the first time, and it wasn't the last time that this occurred, but I have no vivid recollection of that event.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're still in private session, can the Court please produce 1D2993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. We are now in open session. Would you like to go into private session?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, for this document only. The document should not be broadcast, and we should be in private session for the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: (redacted) [Confidentiality partially lifted by order of the Chamber]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm for us that there were war tricks played by the Muslim sides to blacken the Serb side in front of the international community in order provoke a possible military intervention? Was that their tactic?

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serbs didn't really need this type of thing to attract attention on their actions. The sniping activities and the shelling of Sarajevo were really taken into account by the international community. Don't forget that there were many journalists present there. So they didn't really need to resort to these type of acts in order to incriminate the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will see what you said about that, and you said that you were aware of all those tricks at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted, and can we go back into open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that shows your habit of making a statement at the end of question and answers. Please refrain from that habit, please. We discussed it in open session. Shall we admit it publicly or under seal? I'm now at a loss.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: As we've gone through this day, what I've been thinking, Your Honours, that we should err on the side of prudence, and perhaps this could go in under seal, and, of course, as I did the last time we had this situation, I'll vet the transcript very shortly after these proceedings are concluded and I could probably deal with this more effectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We will admit it under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D963 under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we go back into open session, Mr. Karadzic? Yes, we'll do that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the Serb side was rightfully afraid of being vilified and blamed for the grounding of a plane, especially of the papal plane? It was common place to blame Serbs for things that had happened or that might have happened; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: What is your question precisely?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, very well. I give up on the question. The question was whether the Serb fear was understandable, that they had every right to be afraid that they could be blamed for the grounding of a plane, because the airport was within the range of both Serbs and Muslims. Do you agree with me that fire could be opened on the airport from both sides, from the Muslim as well as the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: If you mean there might have been risks of manipulation from either side, then I will answer with a yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Something that the Defence has to clarify is something that is contained in 1D2995, which shouldn't be broadcast. Can you look at bullet point 17. It shouldn't be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is this document about?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what we received with this witness. The Prosecution provided us with this, and I'll tell you what batch was this part of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, in the meantime, could you please look at bullet point 17?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just answer my question. This seems to be a page -- page 4 of certain document. Where's the first page?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have to ask Madam Prosecutor that. We received this document in this form to be represented to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's see how we can follow. What is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was in batch 429, and we are now already on 518 batch. So this was batch 429, and only that -- this one page was in that batch. Do you agree that this was the situation, under bullet point 17, and I don't want to read it for you. You can do it yourself. Witness, can you confirm what you read under bullet point 7 [as interpreted], and that is that on the 23rd September, fire was opened on the airport on the 18th August from the same weapon, and all that was within the total exclusion zone?

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: I would like to see the first page of this document. It's difficult for me to take position about a document of which I know nothing, neither the date nor the origin. So I will answer your question when I've seen page number 1 of this document. I cannot really answer with such imprecise -- with such an imprecise document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. ERN number may be helpful. And we don't have any objections to the entire document being admitted. On the 18th of August, fire was opened on the airport, as the document indicates. We will tender the document if we are provided with the entire document, or, alternatively, we would like to tender into evidence only this page, if that can be admitted. As for shooting before the month of September, we will see proof to that. Let's look at the crisis in September. Do you remember the crisis that involved NATO and the Republika Srpska Army in September?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or you can ask -- shall we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just note that the document, 1D2995, is actually the last page of P865.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we upload that document without broadcasting it?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It is exhibited already, so I think my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then we need to put it under seal, because we dealt with it. We -- that should be put under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we in open session? Right? We are?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session, waiting for that document to be uploaded.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This shouldn't be broadcast. I believe that what we showed is on page 4. Since the document has been admitted, we don't have to read the entire page, but if the witness needs to look at the entire document, he can read it, but let's look at the fourth page. I am speaking fast, because we have already spent a lot of time on this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have now seen page number 1, and indeed this is a report from Mr. Akashi, and I confirm that what is written is appropriate, that the paragraph 17 is appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I would like to take a look at the term "random shelling" of Sarajevo. We're talking about the time when the exclusion zone was in force, and in your statement provided on the 21st November 2007, which is 1D3006; 1D3006, page 10, last paragraph. And on page 11, you speak about those three periods during which shelling took place. I believe that you have the statement in French with you. Now let's look at what your documents -- or, rather, the United Nations document -- documents talk about that. Let's look at P1673.

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not see the text on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your statement provided in 2007. I believe that you were provided with a hard copy of that statement only recently.

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: No. I have a document from 2000, and I have the last document which had been drafted, but I do not have the 2006 statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I don't think the accused is asking any question about that statement. The question is coming regarding the document which you are now looking -- seeing on the monitor. Is this the case? This will be the last question for today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right, Your Excellency. However, I'm mentioning the statement, because what is happening is something that the witness calls a random shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, Witness, all the other UN documents indicate that all that was heavy fighting which was started by the Muslim army which forced the Serbs to respond. Can you please look at bullet point 1. On the 18th September, on the eve of the shelling or the NATO air-strikes: "[In English] On the 18th of September, the heaviest fighting since February 1994 erupted inside Sarajevo. The BiH and BSA engaged approximately 300 mortar rounds and 6.000 small-arm mortars. The attack was initiated by the BH Army and was supported by mortars firing from residential area within the city limits centre and -- [No interpretation] [In English] the BH assaulted the Sharpstone feature, BP," and so on and so on. [Interpretation] Let's look then: "[In English] BH assaulted the Sharpstone feature with the probable objective to seize and to block the Serbian logistic road." [Interpretation] And then we have this: "[In English] Unconfirmed reports from the BSA liaison officer said that the BSA lost ground in the Sharpstone area and suffered two dead on five wounded. These initial attacks were followed by a restrained BSA response using heavy weapons." [Interpretation] And then on the following page where it says -- and while we're waiting for page 2, Witness, sir, does this document say that mortar fire was opened on us from the residential area and that we were suffering losses as a result of that mortar fire; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: As for the authenticity of the document, I do not have any problem, and so I hereby say that what is written tallies with the situation and what we wrote down at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It says here: "[In English] The BSA responded targeting the Zetra stadium, the Presidency, the area north of the cathedral in Sedrenik. The commander, BH command, called on both sides to immediately cease all military actions or he would be obliged to take all appropriate measures to protect the civilian population of Sarajevo including air-strikes." [Interpretation] Then the last sentence: "[In English] The BH initiated the attack and the BSA's response was both defensive and restrained. The BSA did not withdraw weapons from the WCPs." [Interpretation] You saw the name of the general who sent this report. If need be, we'll go back to page 1. He is a very respectable general, and his estimates and assessments should not be doubted; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ450
utterances.text: I can confirm the authenticity of the document as well as the signature on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have reached the end of today's session. This has been admitted into evidence, and tomorrow we will go back towards the agreement which was signed on the 14th. We want to show you when things went pear shaped between the 14th of February and the beginning of August and who was to blame. Do you remember that you, yourself, confirmed in your statements that the period was good from the time the agreement was signed up to the autumn of 1994, and do you agree that that situation was made worse by the BiH Army as a result of the attacks that they launched?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You told Dr. Karadzic some time ago that he had three minutes. We've spent that time reading the document back that's already in evidence and listening to a speech of Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you answer the question in any event, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the comment from the accused, I do not have any answer to give apart from the fact that I've already talked about how the situation unfolded during my tour of duty, and I have nothing else to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Did you take a look at 65 ter 9658, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I indeed did, and I, as usual, stand corrected, Your Honour. You're quite right. It's not included in the amalgamated document that we produced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you're not tendering it?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, I am not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The hearing is now adjourned for today. We will resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 20th day of January, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.35 p.m.,
